title: How To Send A Letter Home To Parents Redux
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin revisits the third-consequence letter-home strategy from his classroom management plan, clarifying misconceptions and adding practical detail for teachers already using the system. He argues that few teachers proactively explain their management plan to parents, and recommends sending a parent information packet, including a sample letter, home before the end of the second week of school so families are never caught off guard. The piece emphasizes that the student, not the teacher, must hand-deliver and return the signed letter, since this active accountability is central to why the consequence works. Linsin also covers optional heads-up phone calls, how to handle a lost or forgotten letter, and stresses that a well-run classroom should only need six to eight such letters per year. He closes by reframing the letter as a parent's right to know rather than a punitive act.
points: Send a parent information packet, including the classroom management plan and a sample letter, before the end of week two so parents are never blindsided.
Require the misbehaving student to personally hand-deliver and return the signed letter, making it an act of active accountability rather than a passive notice.
Use an optional heads-up phone call or email, especially the first time the consequence is used, and always give just the facts, not opinions.
Keep multiple copies on hand for lost-or-forgotten-letter excuses, and pair a reissued letter with a mandatory heads-up call home.
Treat a letter home as a rare event capped around six to eight per year; frequent letters signal a deeper classroom management problem, not a broken plan.
quotes: To avoid a mountain of headaches and parent complaints, and to greatly increase your chances of getting your letters back the next day, send a classroom management packet home with your students before the end of the second week of school.

A letter home to parents should be a rare occurrence. If you’re sending more than six to eight letters home per year, regardless of where you teach, then the problem isn’t your classroom management plan.

By requiring your students to do something to atone for their misbehavior, by placing a burden of responsibility with them, you provide a concrete way for them to acknowledge their misbehavior and take responsibility for it.
If you do call home, it’s best to call during the day and leave a message. If you happen to get a parent on the phone, say only that the letter is on the way.
If, however, the student says she forgot to give her parents the letter—perhaps testing you to see if you’ll follow through—simply hand her a second copy (always make multiple copies).

A letter home to parents holds students to a maximum level of accountability and fulfills the obligation you have to inform parents whenever their child is behaving in a way that risks his (or her) academic progress.
